# RETRO t3-12553

## What worked
- Neutral brief with dependent-project sources (brightnessctl, systemd, thinkpad_acpi via reviewer choice, pkgs#538) let both reviewers reach the material ThinkPad question independently or on cross-check.
- Cross-examination was decisive: four Opus-only claims were independently confirmed by Sol from source; Sol withdrew its own incorrect fresh-install rollout caveat; Sol's four points were quantified by Opus with a sealed run (two kept as optional/local, two dropped from public).
- Sol source-only run was fast (5.9 min); Opus runtime evidence (mutation control D1, scenario matrix) grounded the public Verified table and test note.

## Friction and process deviations
- Opus reviewer: first listing used `ls -la` (owner-name resolution, ~60 lines) before reading the brief; one early `git grep` printed ~95 lines through `cut -c1-220`. Not presented as complete; disclosed in opus/final.md.
- Sol reviewer: some initial source outputs exceeded the 50-line content limit (final.md and followup-1.md retros).
- Coordinator: first read of team-3.json used a byte truncation (`head -c 1500 | head -40`) to view only identity fields of a 1722-line registry; not a policy/source read, but a projection. Two display-only `cut -c` uses on hash/HTML lines. Read the prior team-3 assignment's `render_html.py` (renderer tooling only, no conclusions) to reuse it.
- Editorial check 1 returned revise: the source-only qualifier for the ThinkPad flow sat only in Test scope. Fixed by adding qualifiers beside each visual; check 2 passed.
- Startup memory: coordinator context contained only AGENTS.md/system policy (process corrections naming other PRs), no prior-PR technical conclusions for this PR. No session-local no-memory control was used for the Opus subagent; not verified beyond that.

## Improvements
- Brief first-call rules could explicitly say "no `ls -l`/`ls -la` before reading the brief" since the subagent's first action preceded reading it; consider putting the rule in the omarchy-reviewer agent definition.
- A shared renderer in review-system/ would avoid copying from another assignment.

## Carry forward
- Firmware-handled keys (thinkpad_acpi reserved mask) are a recurring blind spot for binding-based persistence; checking the kernel input path early is worth it for hardware-motivated PRs.

## Automated AI review

> **Community review:** Independent automated community review, unaffiliated with the Omarchy team, intended to help prepare PRs for their review.

**Verified:** at `7ca8b3d`, a level chosen with Omarchy's keyboard-brightness bindings is saved and put back on unlock and at login, and `off` no longer writes 0 into brightnessctl's save file when the LED is already dark. The PR's new test passes at head, and its behavioral section fails on the base commit, so it exercises the new behavior.

```text
Scenario (synthetic brightnessctl model, user chose level 2)     base   head
firmware raised the LED to 3 on resume, then blank + unlock         3      2
blank fired twice while already dark, then unlock                   0      2
reboot, login unit runs with a saved level                          -      2
```

Three points look worth addressing, mainly around the ThinkPad case the PR is aimed at.

### Built-in ThinkPad keyboard-light key never updates the saved level

The state file is written only by `up`, `down` and `cycle`, which run from the `XF86KbdBrightness*` / `XF86KbdLightOnOff` bindings in `default/hypr/bindings/media.lua`. On ThinkPads, upstream `thinkpad_acpi` lets the firmware handle the keyboard-light key: the key is in `hotkey_reserved_mask`, so no key event reaches Hyprland, and the driver only notifies the LED class of the new level. The sequence below is derived from upstream kernel and brightnessctl source; it was not observed on a ThinkPad.

```text
built-in keyboard-light key on a ThinkPad (default thinkpad_acpi config)
  firmware changes the LED
  thinkpad_acpi: key event masked, LED notifies brightness_hw_changed
  Hyprland binding: not triggered
  ~/.local/state/omarchy/keyboard-backlight: not written
reboot + login
  omarchy-keyboard-backlight.service -> restore
    no state file -> brightnessctl -r -> no save file in the new runtime dir
    LED stays at the firmware boot level
```

**Impact:** on the hardware named in the PR description, a level set with the built-in key is not restored at login, and a firmware reset to a nonzero level on resume behaves as before this change. Only the repeated-blank case improves there.

**Suggested change:** confirm how the level was set on the tested ThinkPad. Optional approaches: record firmware-driven changes (for example by watching the LED's `brightness_hw_changed` attribute where the driver provides it), or document that persistence covers levels set through Omarchy's bindings.

### A saved level replaces levels set any other way

Once the state file exists, `restore` always applies it and no longer uses brightnessctl's save from the preceding `off`. `restore` runs at login, on unlock, on lock-screen activity and when an idle cycle is cancelled (`omarchy-system-wake`). Sequence from an isolated run against a synthetic brightnessctl model:

```text
user presses brightness-up to 2      state file = 2
level later changed to 1 another way (firmware key, brightnessctl by hand, another tool)
lock (off) -> unlock (restore)       base: 1    head: 2
```

**Impact:** after a single use of an Omarchy brightness key, every later level set outside the script is reverted on the next wake or login. On ThinkPads this combines with the finding above: the built-in key's changes are undone by an older saved level.

**Suggested change:** if this precedence is intended, note it in the script or the PR description. Tracking firmware-driven changes (previous finding) would also resolve most of this case.

### Fresh installs can permanently miss the login unit

The author asks for this PR to land ahead of omacom/omarchy-pkgs#538, which installs the unit file. If a release contains this change but not that unit file, fresh installs never enable the unit. Sequence traced from the install and migration scripts (source review, not an installed system):

```text
fresh install (unit file not shipped yet)
  first-run: systemctl --user enable --now omarchy-keyboard-backlight.service || true   -> fails silently
  omarchy-provision-user --first-install: marks every shipped migration done, including 1789840930
later update ships the unit file
  omarchy-migrate: 1789840930 already marked -> skipped
  graphical-session.target.wants/: no link -> login restore never runs
```

Existing installs recover, because the migration's fallback symlink becomes valid once the unit ships.

**Impact:** fresh installs in that window keep working unlock restore but never get login restore, with no later repair.

**Suggested change:** ship both changes in the same release, or have a later migration enable the unit when it is missing.

**Optional hardening:** `persist_brightness` runs even when `brightnessctl ... set` fails (brightnessctl 0.5.1 exits 1). A synthetic failed write left the LED at 1 and the saved level at 2, which the next restore then applied. Persisting only after a successful `set` avoids this.

**Optional test improvement:** in `test/shell.d/keyboard-backlight-test.sh`, the bare `! grep -F 'restore-persisted' ...` and `! grep -F 'dbus-monitor' ...` lines can never fail, because Bash exempts `!`-inverted commands from `set -e`. A mutated script containing both strings still passed the full test. Writing them as `if grep -qF ...; then fail "..."; fi` makes them effective.

---

## Review information

**Test scope:** source review of the changed files, their callers, brightnessctl 0.5.1, systemd v262, upstream Linux `thinkpad_acpi`, and omacom/omarchy-pkgs#538. Isolated command-only runs of the PR's test, mutation controls, base/head scenarios against a brightnessctl model written from the 0.5.1 source, and the migration and first-run scripts against a stubbed `systemctl`. No real hardware, sysfs LED, logind or desktop session was used; the ThinkPad behavior is established from kernel source, not observed on a device.

**AI process:** Opus 5.5 Medium coordination and synthesis, independent Opus 5.5 Xhigh and GPT 6 Sol Xhigh technical assessments with targeted cross-checks of each other's claims, Opus 5.5 Medium editorial check.

**Opt out:** To stop receiving these reviews, reply to this comment saying so.
